title: Psychiatric aspects of pain.
abstract: Psychological and emotional factors may determine, or greatly influence, the experience of pain. A review is presented of the concept of the pain prone patient, and the relationships between personality and pain. The importance of an understanding of the psychological meaning of pain is stressed in considering management strategies. Particular attention is directed to depression, anxiety, behavioural approaches and the placebo response. The interaction between the patient in pain and the doctor is discussed in relation to the doctor's needs.

screening.rationale: Narrative review of psychiatric aspects of pain that explicitly devoted particular attention to the placebo response, making placebo phenomena a substantive focus of the paper.

classification.summary: Reviewed psychological contributors to pain and discussed depression, anxiety, behavioural approaches, and gave particular attention to the placebo response and physician–patient interactions.

title: Positive and reverse placebo effects as a function of differences in cues used in self-perception.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

screening.rationale: No abstract or methods available; title names placebo effects but insufficient information to confirm placebo/nocebo was the study's primary focus or the experimental design met inclusion criteria.

classification.summary: Insufficient information in the record to confirm whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were the primary focus; title suggested an experimental study of positive and reverse placebo effects related to self-perception cues.

title: Experimental designs, expectancy effects, and hypnotic analgesia.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title indicates focus on expectancy and hypnotic analgesia but insufficient information to determine whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were an explicit empirical focus or a conceptual review.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title suggested the paper addressed experimental designs and expectancy effects in hypnotic analgesia, but details were unavailable to judge focus on placebo/nocebo empirically.

title: Classical conditioning: induction of luteinizing hormone and testosterone secretion in anticipation of sexual activity.
abstract: A classical conditioning paradigm was used to demonstrate that male rats can learn to secrete luteinizing hormone and testosterone in anticipation of sexual activity. Sexually naïve males were exposed to a neutral stimulus and then to a sexually receptive female once daily. After exposure to the paired stimuli for 14 trials, the neutral stimulus was as effective as the female in triggering luteinizing hormone and testosterone secretion. These findings provide two novel perspectives on the control of reproductive hormone secretion in male rats: (i) environmental cues, which males learn to associate with sexual activity, induce the secretion of hormones that regulate pituitary-testis function, and (ii) classical conditioning may be used as a noninvasive method to evoke functional alterations in the secretion of luteinizing hormone and presumably the neuroendocrine pathways that mediate its release.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment explicitly studied classical conditioning of neuroendocrine (LH and testosterone) responses, matching placebo/nocebo mechanism criteria (classical conditioning in animals).

classification.summary: Demonstrated in male rats that a neutral cue paired with sexual opportunity evoked anticipatory luteinizing hormone and testosterone secretion after conditioning.
classification.key_finding: Found that after 14 pairings a conditioned stimulus alone triggered LH and testosterone secretion in male rats.

title: Social class and treatment expectations of hospitalized psychiatric patients.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and the title suggests treatment expectations but it's unclear whether placebo/nocebo or expectations about treatment context were a primary focus.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title indicated the study examined associations between social class and hospitalized psychiatric patients' treatment expectations.

title: Conditioning and extinction of tolerance to the hypothermic effect of ethanol in rats.
journal: Journal of comparative and physiological psychology

screening.rationale: Title indicates an animal experiment manipulating contextual cues to produce conditioned tolerance/extinction to ethanol hypothermia, which is a classical-conditioning model of placebo-like responses.

classification.summary: Found that rats acquired and showed extinction of conditioned tolerance to ethanol-induced hypothermia following contextual conditioning.
classification.key_finding: Conditioned tolerance to ethanol's hypothermic effect was learned and extinguished in rats.

title: Plasma glucose levels increase after partial hypophysectomy (ACTH removal) and sham surgery in the spiny dogfish shark (Squalus acanthias).

screening.rationale: Title reports physiological changes after sham surgery in an animal experiment, indicating sham/placebo response was an explicit focus (comparison of hypophysectomy and sham surgery).

classification.summary: Found that plasma glucose increased after both partial hypophysectomy and sham surgery in the spiny dogfish shark (Squalus acanthias).
classification.key_finding: Sham surgery produced a measurable increase in blood glucose comparable to partial hypophysectomy.

title: Placebos in clinical trials of duodenal ulcer: the end of an era?

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper addresses the role/ethics of placebos in duodenal ulcer clinical trials, so placebo is the main subject (placebo science/ethics/commentary).

classification.summary: Commented on the ethics and role of placebo use in clinical trials for duodenal ulcer and whether such use remained appropriate.

title: Principal and differential effects of haoperidol and placebo treatments upon speech disfuluencies in stutterers.
journal: Journal of speech and hearing research
abstract: Fourteen stutterers completed a double-blind crossover study of the effects of Haloperidol and Placebo treatments upon their speech disfluencies. Although clearly not clinically effective, Haloperidol had a statistically significant effect upon reducing disfluency frequency and increasing speaking rate. For most subjects, drug-related reductions in disfluency severity resulted from a decrement in whole-word and phrase repetition, interjection, and revision-type disfluencies rather than from fewer part-word (elemental) repetitions and prolongations of sound or of silence. Neurotic personality profile correlated positively with an overall placebo effect, and there was a positive correlation between abnormal EEG and the drug effect. These findings are discussed in light of the nature of speech disfluency and stuttering and Haloperidol's biochemical and behavioral actions.

screening.rationale: Although a drug-versus-placebo efficacy trial, the paper reported and analyzed an overall placebo effect and its correlation with neurotic personality, making placebo response an analytic focus.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind crossover trial of haloperidol versus placebo in 14 stutterers and reported drug benefits alongside a measurable placebo effect that correlated with neurotic personality and EEG abnormalities.
classification.key_finding: Found a significant drug effect on disfluency and speaking rate; neuroticism correlated positively with the magnitude of the placebo effect.

title: The therapeutics of placebo.
abstract: The use of placebo is not old-fashioned, ineffective or unethical. It requires an ongoing, trusting relationship between the physician and the patient. Deception of the patient and self-deception must be avoided. Under these conditions, there are specific situations in which placebo is the treatment of choice.

screening.rationale: Narrative clinical article focused on the ethics and clinical use of placebo as the main subject (placebo science), not an efficacy trial.

classification.summary: Discussed ethical and clinical considerations for using placebos in practice, arguing they can be appropriate when trust and non-deception are maintained.

title: Response to aerosol salbutamol, SCH 1000, and placebo in cystic fibrosis.
abstract: The responses of 20 patients with cystic fribrosis to a B2 agonist, salbutamol, to an anticholinergic agent, SCH 1000, and to a placebo containing difluorodichloroethane and soya lecithin delivered by metered aerosol were compared. Flow rates decreased significantly after placebo (p < 0.05). FEV1 increased significantly after salbutamol (p < 0.05), but the degree of these changes was small. There was a small but significant increase in FVC but no change in flow rates after SCH 1000. Specific conductance increased significantly (p < 0.01) after both salbutamol and SCH 1000. Thoracic gas volume remained unchanged with both drugs and placebo. Four of 20 patients had a clinically significant increase in flow rates with SCH 1000 and three with salbutamol. The consistent increases in sGaw coupled with minimal changes in flow rates, suggest that the physiological effects of both agents is to increase the compressibility of the airway. The results after placebo demonstrate the increased airway reactivity to irritants in cystic fibrosis. In view of this, attention should be paid to the possible irritant effects of inhaled medications.

screening.rationale: An empirical controlled trial reported and analyzed physiological responses to a placebo aerosol (significant decreases in flow rates), so the placebo response was an object of study.

classification.summary: Compared salbutamol, SCH 1000, and an aerosol placebo in 20 cystic fibrosis patients and found significant decreases in flow rates after placebo, indicating airway reactivity to inhaled irritants.
classification.key_finding: Placebo aerosol produced a significant decrease in flow rates (p < 0.05), suggesting irritant-induced airway reactivity in cystic fibrosis.

title: Mental health attitudes and treatment expectations as treatment variables.
abstract: Evaluated 60 patients just before their initial assessment in a community mental health clinic. A series of questions about mental health attitudes and treatment expectation were asked each patient. The Psychiatric Evaluation Form was administered both before evaluation and after five treatment visits. Patients with harsh, pessimistic views about mental illness had more severe psychopathology and did less well over the period of follow-up. Expectation of medication was associated strongly with lower education, greater severity of illness, lower satisfaction with treatment, greater frequency of dropping out of treatment, and less improvement.

screening.rationale: Empirical study that examined patients' treatment expectations and showed associations with clinical outcomes and dropout, making expectation a substantive treatment-variable of interest for placebo science.

classification.summary: Assessed 60 community mental health patients' attitudes and treatment expectations and found pessimistic attitudes and expectation of medication predicted worse symptom course, lower satisfaction, and higher dropout over five visits.
classification.key_finding: Expectation of medication was associated with greater baseline severity, lower satisfaction, higher dropout, and less improvement over follow-up.

title: Autonomic and behavioral effects of dextroamphetamine and placebo in normal and hyperactive prepubertal boys.
abstract: The hypothesis is tested that the response to dextroamphetamine in terms of activity, attention, impulsivity, and autonomic activity is similar in normal (N) and hyperactive (H) children. Fourteen N and 15 H boys had skin conductance (SC), heart rate (HR), and finger temperature (ST) recorded during rest, presentation of eight 75-dB tones, and a reaction time (RT) procedure on three occasions: off drug (Day 1) and after ingestion (double-blind) of placebo and of .5 mg/kg dextroamphetamine. Both N and H groups showed drug effects, compared to placebo, of reduced motor activity and impulsivity, improved attention (RT), increased HR and HR slowing during RT foreperiods, and decreased ST. Both groups also had decreases in SC responsivity but in different parts of the test. Placebo compared to Day 1 produced increased activity and autonomic "arousal" but no change in Rt. Stimulant drugs thus have similar behavioral and autonomic effects in both N and H boys, but the beneficial effects on behavior do not depend critically on increases in arousal.

screening.rationale: Within-subject trial included a placebo condition and compared placebo to an off-drug baseline, reporting placebo-related increases in activity and autonomic arousal (placebo response analyzed).

classification.summary: Found that placebo ingestion, compared to an off-drug baseline, produced increased motor activity and autonomic arousal but no change in reaction time; stimulant drug produced behavioral and autonomic changes.
classification.key_finding: Placebo increased activity and autonomic arousal versus baseline in 29 prepubertal boys (14 controls, 15 hyperactive).

title: Disulfiram implantation: a trial using placebo implants and two types of controls.
abstract: Both disulfiram and placebo implant patients abstained longer and had more intense disulfiram-ethanol reactions than did two control groups.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial that directly compared placebo implants to control groups and reported placebo-arm outcomes (abstinence, reactions), so placebo effects/responses were an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized trial of disulfiram implants found that patients receiving placebo implants abstained longer and showed more intense disulfiram–ethanol reactions than two control groups.
classification.key_finding: Placebo implant patients had longer abstinence and greater disulfiram–ethanol reaction intensity than two control groups.

title: The potent placebo.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and only title/MeSH terms indicate discussion of placebo, so insufficient information to judge whether it reported empirical placebo/nocebo effects or was a review/commentary.

classification.summary: Insufficient information in the record to determine methods or results; titled 'The potent placebo' (1980) and indexed with Placebos, Intractable Pain, and Nursing Care, suggesting a discussion of placebo in pain/nursing contexts.

title: Why does migraine improve during a clinical trial? Further results from a trial of cervical manipulation for migraine.
journal: Australian and New Zealand journal of medicine
abstract: It is generally accepted that migraine is sensitive to intervention, whether in a treatment situation or in a clinical trial, and a "placebo effect" is often suggested. The influence of a number of non-specific therapeutic ingredients was examined in a recent six-month trial of cervical manipulation for migraine, and results of a 20-month follow-up are reported. During the trial migraine attacks reduced significantly by 28%, and reduced a further 19% up to the follow-up period. The possibility of a trial effect, whereby improvement might stem from circumstances of the trial, was dismissed as an explanation for improvement. There was some evidence to suggest that placebo influences made a slight contribution to improvement, with sex, social class and subjects' optimism about the therapist at the initial treatment being weakly associated with initial improvement. The possibility that improvement levels reflected spontaneous improvement in migraine symptoms is suggested. If this possibility proves valid, clinical trials assessing migraine therapies should be designed so as to consider the natural course of migraine. Degree of improvement at follow-up could be predicted clearly from degree of improvement during the treatment phase and from degree of improvement at the end of the trial. This appears to be important to manipulative therapists who appear to practise without the benefit of valid predictors of response to therapy.

screening.rationale: Empirical RCT that specifically examined non-specific/placebo influences and predictors of improvement in a migraine trial, so placebo phenomena were a substantive object of analysis.

classification.summary: Reported that migraine attacks decreased during a 6-month cervical manipulation trial and further at 20-month follow-up, with some evidence that placebo influences and patient optimism weakly contributed to initial improvement.
classification.key_finding: Found a 28% reduction in attacks during the trial and a further 19% by follow-up, with weak associations between initial improvement and optimism about the therapist, sex, and social class.

title: Topical ether and herpes simplex labialis.
abstract: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 51 patients with recurrent herpes simplex labialis were treated with topical ether or placebo within 24 hours of onset of a lesion. There was no noteworthy difference between groups given ether and placebo in progression of lesions, healing time, duration or intensity of pain, and duration or quantity of virus excretion. The ether also failed to reduce appreciably lesion virus titer, even when lesions were cultured immediately after topical application. Despite these results, 75% of the patients receiving ether and 77% of those receiving placebo reported effective reduction of the severity and duration of lesions. The marked placebo effect in the treatment of recurrent herpes infection helps to emphasize the need for objective measurements and placebo-controlled studies.

screening.rationale: Randomized, double-blind trial reported substantial placebo-arm subjective improvement and discussed the placebo effect, so placebo response was a substantive object of analysis.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial compared topical ether with placebo in 51 adults with recurrent herpes labialis and found no objective benefit of ether while both groups reported high subjective improvement, highlighting a marked placebo response.
classification.key_finding: 75% of ether and 77% of placebo recipients reported reduced severity/duration despite no objective differences in healing or viral excretion.

title: Diagnosis is treatment.
abstract: The diagnostic process not only paves the way for treatment, but also functions as a type of treatment itself. Both behavioral and physical problems can respond to diagnosis properly used as a therapeutic tool. The role of diagnosis in dealing with psychological problems focuses on the ascription of meaning to psychological symptoms through proper diagnosis and effective sharing of that with the patient. The placebo effect is used as a model of how belief and understanding about physical symptoms (derived from the diagnosis) constitute treatment. Finally, it is shown that the meaning which the physician assigns to the disease affects recovery, and a "meaning model" of illness is derived and expanded.

screening.rationale: Paper developed a conceptual 'meaning model' using the placebo effect as a central explanatory model for diagnosis-as-treatment, so placebo science is the main subject (theory/commentary).

classification.summary: Argued that diagnosis can function therapeutically by ascribing meaning and shaping patient beliefs, using the placebo effect as a model for how physician communication and meaning influence recovery.

title: A conditioned response model of the placebo effect predictions from the model.
abstract: A model of the placebo response as a conditioned response (CR) is presented and predictions from this model are listed. Through association with active ingredients (UCS), neutral (CS) places, persons, procedures, and things can come to acquire the ability to reduce pain, anxiety, and depressive responses. One major counterintuitive prediction from the model is that therapists who routinely use active ingredients (UCS) or powerful drugs will get stronger placebo effects than those who routinely use "inert" ingredients (CS) or weak drugs. Developmentally, placebo responding appears to involve two successive conditioning stages, which may involve first the left and later the right hemisphere in right-handed subjects. The relationship between placebo responding and hypnotizability is discussed.

screening.rationale: Paper proposed and discussed a conditioned-response model of the placebo effect and made explicit predictions about placebo responding, making placebo mechanisms the primary focus (theory/model paper).

classification.summary: Proposed a conditioned-response model of the placebo effect, listed testable predictions about how cues, therapists, and prior drug use shape placebo analgesia, anxiety and depressive responses.

title: Placebo: deception or potent therapy?

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate a conceptual/ethical discussion of placebo use in clinical practice, fitting 'placebo science' commentary inclusion (placebo as main subject).

classification.summary: Discussed whether using placebos constitutes deception or can be a legitimate, potent therapy in clinical practice.

title: Conditioned drug effects to d-amphetamine- and morphine-induced motor acceleration in mice: experimental approach for placebo effect.
abstract: Ninety-two mice were divided into 2 groups and 2.5 mg/kg of d-amphetamine sulfate was given to one group, and 10 mg/kg of morphine hydrochloride to the other, at daily intervals. These two groups were then further divided into flicking light-presented and non-presented groups. The acute effects of the drugs on the ambulatory activity of each mouse were observed for 180 min after the drug administration. The motor-accelerating effect of both drugs was progressively enhanced with repeated administration. After the drugs were administered 10 times, physiological saline was given subcutaneously to the mice and the motor-accelerating effect of the drugs could be observed for a short time, especially in the flicking light-presented groups. This effect disappeared after repeated administration of saline solution at daily intervals for 6 days. Thus, the motor-accelerating effect produced by saline is considered to have been elicited as the result of conditioning between the conditioned stimuli (flicking light and other environmental factors) and drug effects.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment used Pavlovian conditioning with drug administration and saline test to elicit conditioned (placebo-like) motor effects, so placebo phenomena were the explicit object of study (mechanisms of conditioned placebo effect).

classification.summary: Found that after repeated amphetamine or morphine administration paired with a flickering light, saline produced short-lived motor-accelerating (conditioned) responses in mice, which extinguished after repeated saline.
classification.key_finding: Conditioned motor acceleration was elicited by saline in mice previously paired with amphetamine or morphine, especially when a flickering light cue had been presented.

title: The role of attributions of responsibility in the facilitation of unusual experiential states during alpha training: an analysis of the biofeedback placebo effect.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly analyses the 'biofeedback placebo effect' and the role of attributions in alpha-training, indicating placebo phenomena were the paper's focus despite no abstract being available.

classification.summary: Examined how attributions of responsibility influenced facilitation of unusual experiential states during alpha biofeedback training and analyzed the biofeedback placebo effect.

title: Chronic back pain: electromyographic, motion and behavioral assessments following sympathetic nerve blocks and placebos.
abstract: Twenty patients with chronic low back pain received 12 lumbar sympathetic injections, in a series of 6 with bupivacaine and a series of 6 with saline. Changes in subjective pain intensity, EMG from paravertebral muscles, joint ranges of mobility, and daily activity levels were measured at multiple intervals throughout treatment and at 3 monthly follow-up intervals. The MMPI was administered before treatment, after treatment and at 3-month follow-up. Results revealed significant reductions in subjective pain intensity lasting 1 month after treatment which were not significantly different during bupivacaine and saline injection periods. Patients' MMPI profiles were indicative of reduced depression and an increase in ability to manage their lives. No significant changes were recorded with respect to EMG, joint range of mobility, or daily activity levels. Results were discussed in terms of a massive placebo effect and analgesia obtained through hyperstimulation of various tissue structures. They are consistent with the hypothesis that central postsynaptic mechanisms were predominant in these patients' chronic back pain states. Because subjective pain relief did not independently produce increasing function, it was recommended that deep analgesic injections or other pain relieving techniques be matched with behavior modification leading to functional rehabilitation.

screening.rationale: Within-subject crossover of active (bupivacaine) versus saline injections reported placebo-equivalent subjective analgesia and discussed a large placebo response, making placebo response a focal finding.

classification.summary: Found that subjective pain decreased similarly after bupivacaine and saline lumbar sympathetic injections, while EMG, mobility, and daily activity showed no change, pointing to a large placebo-related analgesia.
classification.key_finding: Subjective pain reductions lasted about one month and did not differ between active and saline injection periods.

title: Placebo usage in clinical trials of life-saving drugs. Summary of discussion results.
journal: Progress in clinical and biological research

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper's main subject is the use and ethics of placebos in trials (placebo science/ethics), so it meets inclusion as placebo_science_other despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Summarized discussion findings about the use of placebos in clinical trials of life-saving drugs, focusing on ethical and practical considerations.

title: Placebo usage in clinical trials of lifesaving drugs.
journal: Progress in clinical and biological research

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses placebo usage in clinical trials and associated ethics/design issues, indicating placebo is the paper's main subject despite no abstract being available.

classification.summary: Discussed the ethical and methodological issues of using placebos in clinical trials of lifesaving drugs, including informed consent and physician–patient relations.

title: Placebo usage in clinical trials of life-saving drugs.
journal: Progress in clinical and biological research

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate the paper's main subject is the use and ethics of placebos in clinical trials (placebo science), though no abstract was available to confirm details.

classification.summary: Discussed the use and ethical implications of placebos in clinical trials of life-saving drugs, including issues of informed consent and double-blind methodology.

title: Comparative trial of clomipramine and placebo in the treatment of terminal pain.
journal: The Journal of international medical research
abstract: The use of antidepressants, and other psychotropic drugs, in the management of terminal pain is well established in clinical practice. However, few attempts have been made to test the value of such treatment in the setting of the double-blind controlled clinical trial. This paper describes an attempt, using clomipramine and a matching placebo, which failed. The difficulties encountered and possible reasons for failure are discussed.

screening.rationale: Abstract describes a double-blind drug versus placebo efficacy trial but gives insufficient information to determine whether the paper analyzed placebo effects/responses rather than only testing the active drug.

classification.summary: Reported a double-blind randomized comparison of clomipramine versus matching placebo for terminal pain, described as failing with discussion of encountered difficulties.

title: On chronic effects of different drugs on the higher nervous activity in man. Placebo.
journal: Acta Universitatis Palackianae Olomucensis Facultatis Medicae
journal_abbrev: Acta Univ Palacki Olomuc Fac Med

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms mention placebo and conditioning in humans but no abstract or methods are available to determine whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were an explicit focus or experimentally isolated.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title indicated investigation of chronic drug effects and placebos on higher nervous activity in humans, but methods and whether placebo effects were a primary focus were unclear.

title: A placebo for the doctor.

screening.rationale: Historical/journal commentary whose main subject appears to be the placebo concept and its history, so it fits placebo_science_other inclusion (history/conceptual piece).

classification.summary: Reviews historical and conceptual aspects of placebo use in medicine (United States) as a commentary.

title: Effects of placebo versus guanabenz on hypertensive out-patients.
journal: The Journal of international medical research
abstract: The objectives of this study were two-fold: (1) 1 4-week multicentre, randomized, double-blind efficacy comparison of placebo and guanabenz acetate, a new centrally acting antihypertensive drug, in 168 hypertensive out-patients and (2) a more accurate determination of the incidence of drug-related, non-specific side-effects. Both treatment groups were comparable: 68% female, 63% black, mean age 53 years; 57% mild, 32% moderate, 11% moderately severe hypertensives. Seventy-six placebo patients completed 4 weeks and had a mean supine diastolic blood pressure (SDBP) decrease from 105 to 101 mm Hg (p < 0.01). Seventy-nine guanabenz patients completing 4 weeks had a mean SDBP decrease from 104 to 92 mm Hg (p < 0.01). All of the placebo responses and 10/12 mm Hg of the guanabenz response occurred during Week 1. Clinically significant individual SDBP decreases occurred in thirty-one (41%) placebo and fifty-five (70%) guanabenz-treated patients (p < 0.01). Mean daily guanabenz dose was 24 mg. Drug-related biochemical or electrocardiographic abnormalities were absent. Side-effects of sedation and dry mouth were recorded two and three times more frequently, respectively, in guanabenz as compared to placebo patients. Side-effects usually occurred within Week 1 and diminished in incidence thereafter. Consequently, in these patients it appeared that: (1) guanabenz was an effective, well-tolerated drug, (2) placebo effects on efficacy were significant, occurred early and remained stable, and (3) placebo and guanabenz side-effects were mainly sedation and dry mouth.

screening.rationale: Reported and analyzed placebo-arm blood pressure change and incidence of side-effects in the placebo group, meeting inclusion for placebo_response and nocebo_response analyses.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial compared guanabenz versus placebo in 168 hypertensive outpatients and reported significant placebo-arm blood pressure reductions and placebo-group side-effects (sedation, dry mouth).
classification.key_finding: Placebo group mean supine diastolic BP fell from 105 to 101 mmHg (p<0.01); 41% had clinically significant decreases and some side-effects were reported in the placebo arm.

title: Responders and nonresponders to chlordiazepoxide and placebo: a discriminant function analysis.

screening.rationale: Title names responders to placebo as an explicit analytic focus (discriminant analysis of chlordiazepoxide and placebo responders), so placebo response is an object of study.

classification.summary: Analyzed characteristics that distinguished responders and nonresponders to chlordiazepoxide and placebo using discriminant function analysis in an anxiety clinical trial.

title: Alcoholic beverages and their placebos: an empirical evaluation of expectancies.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title indicates placebo beverages/expectancies but insufficient information to confirm placebo/nocebo was the explicit focus or the design.

title: Analysis of single-double blind procedures, maintenance of placebo effects and drug induced dyskinesia with mentally retarded persons.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly named analysis of maintenance of placebo effects and single-vs-double blind procedures, indicating placebo phenomena were a stated focus (rule 4/1).

classification.summary: Reported analysis of single- versus double-blind procedures and maintenance of placebo effects, alongside drug-induced dyskinesia, in adults with intellectual disability.

title: Circadian placebo and ACTH effects on urinary cortisol in arthritics.
abstract: The effect of placebo and ACTH-1-17 (Synchrodyn, Hoechst) upon urinary free cortisol was examined at 5 different circadian stages on 10 men with Steinbrocker Stage II-III rheumatoid arthritis. A mean cosinor analysis of urinary cortisol data from the subjects prior to treatment with either ACTH or placebo revealed a statistically highly-significant rhythm. A circadian variation in a response of urinary free cortisol to a placebo was also seen. Moreover, the response of the midline-estimating statistic of rhythm (rhythm-adjusted circadian average) of urinary free cortisol to ACTH-1-17 by patients with rheumatoid arthritis is circadian rhythmic. This reactivity rhythm is out of phase with the spontaneous rhythm in urinary cortisol acrophases-in the tests limited thus far to midsummer. The further assessment of the circadian component in the context of broader interactions by rhythms with other frequencies in various conditions in health and disease is warranted by the demonstration of rhythms here presented for men with rheumatoid arthritis.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly measured physiological responses to a placebo (urinary cortisol) and reported circadian variation in the placebo response, making placebo response a primary object of analysis.

classification.summary: Measured urinary free cortisol responses to placebo and ACTH at five circadian stages in 10 men with rheumatoid arthritis and found a circadian variation in the cortisol response to placebo.
classification.key_finding: Found circadian variation in urinary cortisol responses to placebo and to ACTH-1-17; placebo produced measurable cortisol changes varying by circadian stage.

title: The effect of alcohol and placebo on affective reactions of social drinkers to a procedure designed to induce depressive affect anxiety and hostility.
abstract: Randomly assigned 33 males to one of three alcohol conditions: High dose (two groups), placebo, and no-dose. All Ss after drinking performed a pseudo test of intelligence. One group of high-dose Ss received feedback that indicated an extremely good performance on the intelligence task (Incentive Gain), while all other Ss received extremely poor performance scores (Incentive Loss). Analysis of pre-post feedback scores on the Multiple Affect Adjective Check List indicated differential effect of alcohol and placebo with no change of depressive affect in the two high-dose alcohol groups, but an increase in placebo Ss. Furthermore, incentive loss high-dose Ss rated themselves as significantly more intoxicated than did incentive gain high-dose Ss. The results are discussed in terms of attribution for success and failure, cognitions and depressive affect, and tension reduction models of alcoholism.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial explicitly contrasted placebo beverage against a no-dose control to test alcohol/placebo effects on affect, so placebo effect was an explicit experimental focus.

classification.summary: Randomized social drinkers to high-dose alcohol, placebo beverage, or no-dose; found placebo participants showed increased depressive affect after feedback while alcohol groups did not.
classification.key_finding: Placebo beverage recipients increased depressive affect (MAACL) relative to no-dose controls, suggesting expectancy/attribution effects; N=33.
